title: Polar Animals Ice Play
strapline: Animals frozen into blocks of ice, and warm water to rescue them with — science that feels like a mission.
intent: Children explore Arctic and Antarctic habitats and how animals are adapted to the cold.
Melting ice is a first, vivid experience of a material changing state.
Squeezing droppers and wielding spoons builds real fine motor strength.
A rescue mission gives a scientific investigation a purpose children care about.
Predicting what will melt fastest is early scientific thinking made concrete.
implementation: Freeze small polar animals into blocks or bowls of ice the day before.
Provide warm water in droppers, pipettes, spray bottles and spoons for the rescue.
Add salt and warm water as alternative tools so children can compare methods.
Model using a dropper — squeeze, dip, release — and then step back.
Introduce the vocabulary as they work: freeze, melt, slippery, cold, solid, water.
Talk about penguins, polar bears and seals and how their bodies cope with cold.
Have towels and warm water for hands nearby; cold hands end the investigation early.
key_questions: How could you get the animal out without breaking the ice?
What is happening to the ice? Where is it going?
Which is working faster — the warm water or the spoon?
How do you think a real polar bear keeps warm?
What do you think will be left when we come back after lunch?

impact.text: Children explore materials and change through play — melting, freezing, mixing.
Children make predictions and still ask why.
Children use droppers, spoons and small tools with growing precision.
Children take up and use new scientific vocabulary in their own talk.
Children persist at a tricky task long enough to succeed.
Children handle the animals gently and care about rescuing them.

enhancements: A comparison test — one block in the sun, one in the shade, one in the fridge.
Coloured ice so the melt is visible as it spreads.
A polar small world tray set up alongside for the rescued animals to live in.
A shaving-foam and cotton-wool snow tray for children who dislike cold hands.
A blubber glove experiment — a hand in a bag of fat in cold water.
A recording sheet where children draw the ice at the start, middle and end.

playing_exploring: Children investigate ice with several tools and find their own method.
The rescue is open-ended: any way that works is a good way.
active_learning: Children stay with a slow process, checking back over the session.
Freeing the animal is a goal they set themselves and push towards.
creating_thinking: Children predict which method will be fastest and test it.
They reason about where the ice has gone and why it changed.
